---
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:upper}
$t_{\mathbb{Z}}([0,1])\le 0.422684697505$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:lower}
$t_{\mathbb{Z}}([0,1])\ge 0.422228600019$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:bracket}
$0.4222286000\ \le\ t_{\mathbb{Z}}([0,1])\ \le\ 0.4226846976$. The width of the bracket
drops from $1.39\cdot10^{-3}$ to $4.56\cdot10^{-4}$.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:sym}
The infimum in \eqref{eq:lp} over all finite libraries in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ is attained
in the limit by libraries consisting of integer polynomials in $w=x(1-x)$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
First, an optimal weight assignment may be taken symmetric: if $c$ is feasible
then so is its reflection $c'$, obtained by putting the weight of $Q_j$ on
$Q_j(1-x)$, with the same objective value; and the average $(c+c')/2$ is
feasible with objective at most the average of the two objectives, since the
maximum of an average is at most the average of the maxima. Such a solution
pairs $Q(x)$ and $Q(1-x)$ with equal weight, so the corresponding product is
invariant under $x\mapsto1-x$.

Second, an integer polynomial invariant under $x\mapsto1-x$ is an integer
polynomial in $w$. Indeed, put $u=x-\tfrac12$; the involution becomes
$u\mapsto-u$, so the invariants are the integer polynomials in $u^2$, and
$w=\tfrac14-u^2$, the change of basis between $u^2$ and $w$ being unimodular
over $\mathbb{Z}$ in both directions.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:mono}
Let $R(w)=a\prod_\rho(w-\rho)$ and let $t\in\mathbb{R}$, $H>0$. Then for every
$w\in[t-H,t+H]$,
\[
  \log|R(w)|\ \le\ \log\Bigl(|a|\prod_\rho\bigl(|t-\rho|+H\bigr)\Bigr).
\]
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
$|w-\rho|\le|t-\rho|+H$ for each $\rho$, and $\log$ is increasing.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Bisection of $[0,1/4]$ with the bound above terminates with
\[
  \max_{[0,1/4]}f\ \le\ -1.7222575477025739
\]
after $267\,245$ intervals over $28$ levels, whence
\[
  t_{\mathbb{Z}}([0,1])\ \le\ \exp(-1.7222575477025739/2)\ \le\ 0.422684697505 .
\]
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:transport}
Let $f(x)=\log(x+1)-\sum_j c_j\log|Q_j(x)|\ge m$ on $x>0$ with
$D:=\sum_j c_j\deg Q_j\le1$, an auxiliary function for the absolute length as
in \cite{F14}. Put $y=x/(x+1)$ and
$q_j(y):=(1-y)^{\deg Q_j}\,Q_j\bigl(y/(1-y)\bigr)\in\mathbb{Z}[y]$. Then
\[
  \sum_j c_j\log|q_j(y)|\ +\ (1-D)\log(1-y)\ \le\ -m
  \qquad\text{on }[0,1],
\]
and the total degree of the left-hand side is $D+(1-D)=1$. Thus every such
auxiliary function is an instance of the program \eqref{eq:lp}.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
$x+1=1/(1-y)$ and $Q_j(x)=q_j(y)(1-y)^{-\deg Q_j}$, so
$f=\;-\log(1-y)-\sum_j c_j\log|q_j(y)|+D\log(1-y)$, and $f\ge m$ is the
displayed inequality. The map $x\mapsto y$ carries $(0,\infty)$ onto $(0,1)$.
The column $\log(1-y)$ has degree $1$ and weight $1-D$, and $\sum_j c_j\deg
q_j=D$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:cert}
With the notation above,
\[
  t_{\mathbb{Z}}([0,1])\ \ge\ \exp\Bigl(\min\Bigl\{\ \inf_{[0,1]}A,\ \ -\sum_j c_j\log a_j,\ \ \min_i G_i\ \Bigr\}\Bigr).
\]
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Let $P\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ have degree $n$, root measure $\nu$, leading coefficient of
modulus $e^{nL}$, and $M=\|P\|_{[0,1]}$. Since $\mu$ is a probability measure,
\[
  \log M\ \ge\ \int\log|P|\,d\mu\ =\ n\Bigl(L+\int U_\mu\,d\nu\Bigr)
\]
by Fubini. Write $P=\prod_i (Q^{(i)})^{e_i}$ over its distinct irreducible
factors, $\nu=\sum_i m_i\nu^{(i)}$ with $m_i\ge0$, $\sum_i m_i=1$, and
$L=\sum_i m_iL^{(i)}$. Then $L+\int U_\mu d\nu=\sum_i m_iH_i$ with
$H_i:=L^{(i)}+\int U_\mu\,d\nu^{(i)}$, so it suffices to bound each $H_i$ from
below.

For every library index $j$ with $Q_j\ne Q^{(i)}$ the resultant
$\operatorname{Res}(Q^{(i)},Q_j)$ is a nonzero integer, so $|\operatorname{Res}(Q^{(i)},Q_j)|\ge1$ and,
taking logarithms and normalising,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:res}
  d_j\,L^{(i)}+\int\log|Q_j|\,d\nu^{(i)}\ \ge\ 0 .
\end{equation}
Subtracting \eqref{eq:res} with the weights $c_j\ge0$ from $H_i$,
\[
  H_i\ \ge\ L^{(i)}\Bigl[1-\!\!\sum_{j:\,Q_j\ne Q^{(i)}}\!\!c_jd_j\Bigr]
  +\int\Bigl[U_\mu-\!\!\sum_{j:\,Q_j\ne Q^{(i)}}\!\!c_j\log|Q_j|\Bigr]d\nu^{(i)} .
\]
Two cases occur, and they are exhaustive.

If $Q^{(i)}$ is not in the library, both sums run over all $j$: the bracket is
$A$, the coefficient is $1-B\ge0$, and $L^{(i)}\ge0$ because $a^{(i)}\ge1$;
hence $H_i\ge\inf_\mathbb{C} A$.

If $Q^{(i)}=Q_i$ lies in the library, the term $j=i$ must be omitted, since
$\operatorname{Res}(Q_i,Q_i)=0$ and \eqref{eq:res} is unavailable for it. The coefficient
becomes $1-B+c_id_i$ and the bracket becomes $A+c_i\log|Q_i|$; the resulting
lower bound is exactly $G_i$.

Finally $A$ is harmonic on the Riemann sphere minus $[0,1]$ and the zeros of
the $Q_j$, and tends to $+\infty$ at those zeros, so its infimum over $\mathbb{C}$ is
attained on $[0,1]$ or at infinity, and $A(\infty)=-\sum_j c_j\log a_j$.
Taking the minimum of the three quantities and exponentiating gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
The second case is the whole difficulty. A single polynomial with all roots in
$[0,1]$ gives no lower bound whatsoever, because the near-extremal $P$ are
divisible by precisely those polynomials; this is why the classical
Gorshkov--Wirsing bound is an infimum over an infinite family of pairwise
coprime members. The terms $G_i$ are what pays for divisibility. They are
affine in $(\mu,c)$ jointly, so Theorem \ref{thm:cert} turns the search for the
best certificate into a single semi-infinite linear program in $(\mu,c)$.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:uni}
$\psi_k$ is unimodal on $\mathbb{R}$ with minimum exactly at the midpoint of the
cell. Consequently its minimum over an interval $[t-H,t+H]$ is attained at the
point of that interval closest to the midpoint.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
For a cell $[a,b]$ one has $\psi_k'(x)=\bigl(\log|x-a|-\log|x-b|\bigr)/h_k$,
which vanishes only at $x=(a+b)/2$ and changes sign there.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
The certificate consists of a measure $\mu$ carried by $947$ cells with
explicit edges and a library of $J=206$ polynomials. Lower bounds for $A$ on
subintervals combine Lemma \ref{lem:uni}, which is lossless, with Lemma
\ref{lem:mono} applied to each $\log|Q_j|$ with its measured residual, the
largest being $4.501\cdot10^{-44}$; a rounding allowance $10^{-10}$ is
subtracted throughout. Bisection over $12\,326\,733$ intervals in $33$ levels
gives
\[
  \inf_{[0,1]}A\ \ge\ V:=-0.862208405409 .
\]
The two remaining quantities of Theorem \ref{thm:cert} are checked directly on
the shipped data: $A(\infty)=-0.688183611561\ge V$ and
$\min_iG_i=-0.862208282175\ge V$, the latter with margin $1.23\cdot10^{-7}$.
The budget is $B=0.999999999\le1$. Hence
$t_{\mathbb{Z}}([0,1])\ge e^{V}=0.422228600019$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:ceiling}
Let $\mu_1,\dots,\mu_r$ be probability measures on $[0,1]$ and, for an
irreducible $Q$ with root measure $\nu$ and $L=\log(\mathrm{lead}\,Q)/\deg Q$,
put $H_t(Q)=L+\int U_{\mu_t}d\nu$. Then
\[
  \min_{m\in\Delta}\ \max_{1\le t\le r}\ \sum_i m_i\,H_t(Q^{(i)})
  \ =\ \max_{\lambda\in\Delta}\ \min_i\ H_{\mu_\lambda}(Q^{(i)}) ,
  \qquad \mu_\lambda:=\sum_t\lambda_t\mu_t ,
\]
and $\mu_\lambda$ is again a single admissible probability measure. Hence the
bound obtained from the family $\{\mu_1,\dots,\mu_r\}$ is already attained by
one measure.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
$H_t(Q)$ is affine in $\mu_t$, so $\sum_t\lambda_tH_t(Q)=H_{\mu_\lambda}(Q)$.
The left-hand side is the value of the matrix game with payoff
$\bigl(H_t(Q^{(i)})\bigr)_{i,t}$, and von Neumann's minimax theorem identifies
it with $\max_\lambda\min_i\sum_t\lambda_tH_t(Q^{(i)})$, which is
$\max_\lambda\min_iH_{\mu_\lambda}(Q^{(i)})$. Since $\Delta$ is the simplex,
$\mu_\lambda$ is a probability measure on $[0,1]$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
